newsitem.title: UK: Cap. markets to change insurance - Aon deputy.
newsitem.headline: Cap. markets to change insurance - Aon deputy.

text.p: The global insurance industry will see the introduction of capital markets, further consolidation and growth in technology, an industry chief said on Tuesday.

"The introduction of capital markets into insurance is a reality. It will have an impact on the way we do business. It is more talked about than acted on at the moment, but it won't go away," said Ron Forrest, deputy chairman (Europe and Asia) of insurance broker Aon.
Speaking at the Association of Insurance and Risk Managers (AIRMIC) conference, he added that he expects the distribution chain in insurance to become shorter in the years to come.
"Companies such as Aon, J&H Marsh & McLennan, Zurich and AIG will not tolerate the inefficiencies in the current structure," he said.

"Visionaries such as Pat Ryan, who built Aon but started as an insurer, saw the value of brokers as the key distribution method. The capital can come from anywhere, but the distributors will become the most important factor," he added.
"There is no doubt that there will be more consolidation in the industry, probably more among insurance companies than among brokers," said Forrest.
The global broking industry has been considerably slimmed down by mergers in the last six months, in particular Marsh & McLennan with Johnson & Higgins and Aon with Alexander & Alexander.
Forrest said other key trends would include the growth of self insurance, mutualisation of funds and pooled insurance arrangements.
He added that the growth of technology and insurance transaction systems would also be a major feature of insurance in the future.

"This will pose a question. Brokers in Manchester or Manhattan will be able to place risks with insurance companies anywhere in the world. Does this mean that the insured clients will also be able to do it themselves?"
Forrest said the industry should strive towards greater unity in order to tackle the challenges of the future.
"It is difficult to see how all these issues will be handled in a fragmented industry. Someone has to speak for the industry," he said.
